opus-5.5.text:
I think the question of cost is real, but I'd frame it a bit differently. The question isn't just "how do we make agents cheaper," it's "what is the agent's output actually worth?"

For a chatbot answering a casual question, spending a lot of compute is hard to justify, because the value of each answer is small. But if an agent finishes a real task, like fixing a bug in a large codebase, doing a week's worth of research, or handling a full customer workflow, then the value can be very high. In that setting, spending more on inference isn't a problem, it's a trade. The important thing is that the cost per unit of *useful work* goes down, not that the cost per token goes down.

So I think scaling agents has a few parts.

First, the models and systems will keep getting more efficient. Distillation, better architectures, better hardware. That curve has been very steep, and I expect it to continue. Something that feels expensive today might be ten times cheaper in a year or two.

Second, and I think this matters more, agents need to get better at using compute wisely. Right now a lot of agent compute is wasted: going in circles, retrying the same thing, reading irrelevant context. A good human expert doesn't think harder on every step. They know when to be fast and when to slow down. Agents should learn that too, spending a lot of thinking on the hard decisions and moving quickly through the easy ones. That's partly a training question and partly an environment and evaluation question. If our benchmarks reward only final accuracy and ignore cost, we'll get agents that brute-force everything.

Third, memory and accumulated experience. Today many agents start almost from scratch each time. If an agent can remember what worked, reuse tools it built, and carry context across tasks, then the marginal cost of the next task drops a lot. That's how humans become efficient over a career. I think this "lifelong" side of agents is still very underexplored.

And finally, the product side: find the tasks where value clearly exceeds cost, and start there. You don't need agents to be cheap enough for everything on day one. You need them to be clearly worth it for some things, and then the frontier expands as costs fall and capabilities rise.

So my view is that high compute cost is more a temporary constraint than a fundamental barrier. The deeper question is whether agents can do work that's genuinely valuable. If they can, the economics tend to work themselves out.

r001.rationale: It says the key metric is cost per unit of useful work and that higher inference spending can make sense when the task’s value is high.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with tasks where the agent’s value clearly exceeds its cost, then expanding as costs fall and capabilities rise.

r003.rationale: It discusses spending more reasoning on hard decisions, but does not propose matching model size to task difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think the framing of "compute cost" is actually a bit misleading, because it treats the cost as the fundamental constraint. I'd argue the fundamental constraint is something else, and the cost question resolves itself once you see that.

Let me back up. When people say agents are expensive, they usually mean something like: an agent runs for an hour, makes hundreds of model calls, burns a lot of tokens, and at the end maybe it succeeds, maybe it doesn't. And if you compare that to a single chat response, yes, it's orders of magnitude more. But I think the right comparison is not agent versus chatbot. The right comparison is agent versus the human who would otherwise do that task. If an agent spends twenty dollars of compute to do something that would take a software engineer a full day, that's not expensive. That's absurdly cheap. So the first thing I'd say is: cost per task matters, not cost per token. And cost per task only looks bad right now because success rates on long-horizon tasks are still low. Most of the compute is wasted on trajectories that fail.

So the scaling question really becomes: how do you make the compute productive? And here I think there are three things.

First, the environment matters more than the model. I keep coming back to this. In the first half of AI, we scaled models and the benchmarks were basically static datasets. In the second half, the thing you're scaling is the agent's interaction with an environment, and the environment is where the learning signal comes from. If your environment is poorly designed, if the feedback is sparse or noisy or just wrong, you can throw infinite compute at it and you'll get garbage. A good environment with a clear reward and rich observations lets a relatively small model learn much faster than a huge model in a bad environment. So before you worry about compute scaling, you should worry about whether your agent is in an environment where compute translates into learning.

Second, I think we've underappreciated memory and context engineering relative to raw inference scaling. A lot of the cost in agents comes from re-reading the same context, re-deriving the same facts, re-exploring the same dead ends. Humans don't do this. We have a very efficient prior about what's worth remembering. If agents had good memory, both within a task and across tasks, you'd cut cost dramatically, not by making the model cheaper but by making it do less redundant work. This is less glamorous than scaling laws but I think it's where a lot of the practical gains are.

Third, and this is the one I feel most strongly about, we need to change what we're measuring. Right now almost every benchmark reports accuracy, or pass rate, or something like that, with no notion of cost. So the incentive is to use the biggest model with the most test-time compute, because that maximizes the number. But if a benchmark said: here's the task, here's your budget, do the best you can, you'd see very different research. You'd see people thinking about when to stop, when to ask for help, when to use a cheap model versus an expensive one, how to allocate compute within a trajectory. These are exactly the questions that matter for scaling in practice, and we basically don't study them because the benchmarks don't reward it.

So to directly answer your question: I don't think the path is "make compute cheaper until agents are affordable." Compute will get cheaper, sure, but that's not the interesting part. The interesting part is that an agent which actually solves the task is already cheap relative to the alternative, and the way you get there is better environments, better memory, and evaluation that treats cost as a first-class variable rather than an afterthought. If you do those things, the scaling takes care of itself. If you don't, you'll keep burning money on trajectories that go nowhere.

r001.rationale: The response says cost per task matters and compares an agent’s compute cost with the human effort and value of completing the task.

r002.rationale: It discusses making compute productive through environments, memory, and cost-aware evaluation, but does not prioritize identifying a valuable application before optimizing compute costs.

r003.rationale: It mentions choosing between cheap and expensive models, but does not propose matching model size to application difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what are we getting from that compute? If an agent costs ten times more but solves a problem that previously required hours of human work, that can still be a very good tradeoff. If it spends ten times more just repeating the same mistakes, then scaling isn’t helping.

So I would separate making each step cheaper from making additional steps useful. You can use a smaller model for routine decisions and reserve a stronger model for the difficult parts. But you also need the agent to recognize when it’s making progress, when it should verify something, and when it should stop or ask a person. Otherwise, a longer trajectory just becomes a more expensive failure.

I’d start with bounded tasks where success is measurable. Then you can ask: does giving the agent more compute actually increase the success rate, and is that improvement worth the cost? The goal shouldn’t be maximum autonomy or maximum reasoning on every task. It should be allocating enough computation to get a useful result reliably.

r001.rationale: It says a higher compute cost can be worthwhile if the agent solves valuable work, and recommends weighing success improvement against cost.

r002.rationale: It proposes starting with measurable bounded tasks, but does not prioritize finding a valuable application before optimizing compute costs.

r003.rationale: It recommends using a smaller model for routine decisions and reserving a stronger model for difficult parts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what are we getting for that compute? If an agent costs ten dollars but completes a task that would otherwise take someone several hours, that can be a very good trade. If it costs ten dollars and you still have to check every step and redo the work, then it’s much harder to justify.

So I wouldn’t think of scaling as simply giving every agent more tokens or more steps. We need to make agents better at deciding when to spend compute. A simple task should take a short path. A difficult task might justify more reasoning, trying different approaches, or checking the result. And the agent needs to know when to stop, or when to ask a person for help.

There are really two directions here: make each unit of computation cheaper, and make the computation more useful. The second is especially important for agents, because a long sequence of actions doesn’t necessarily mean progress. I’d rather measure the cost of successfully completing a task than the cost per token. That connects scaling to something users actually care about.

r001.rationale: It compares a ten-dollar agent cost with the value of completing several hours of work and favors measuring cost per successfully completed task.

r002.rationale: It discusses making computation cheaper and more useful, but does not prioritize identifying a valuable application before optimizing compute costs.

r003.rationale: It suggests allocating more reasoning or checks to difficult tasks, but does not propose matching model size to application difficulty.
